question: யவனர் முசிறி பொன்னொடு வந்து கறியொடு பெயரும்
answer: The line quoted appears in a Tamil poem describing Muciri, where it states that ships "தந்த வினைமாண் நன்கலம் பொன்னொடு வந்து கறியொடு பெயரும்" arrived with gold and returned with pepper [S1]. The accompanying published translation renders this as vessels "the masterpieces of the Yavanas [Ionians/Greeks-Romans]" that came to Muciri "arriving with gold and departing with pepper," at a Muciri described as "brimming with prosperity" [S1]. This translation is paired with the Tamil text only by position rather than by matching section numbers, which the source describes as weaker evidence, and the source further notes that Old Tamil is the weakest-supported language in this material, with the English resting on a published translation rather than a directly verified rendering [S1]. A separate account of the same general trading coast, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes the neighbouring port area of Nelkynda and the village of Bacare, noting that ships "drop down on the outward voyage from Nelcynda" to Bacare to load cargo because "the river is full of shoals and the channels are not clear," but this passage does not itself mention Yavanas, gold, or pepper at Muciri [S2]. Thus S1 and S2 both concern the Muziris/Nelkynda trading region, but only S1 makes the specific claim in the quoted line about Yavana ships bringing gold and taking away pepper [S1][S2].

quote_spans.quote: தந்த வினைமாண் நன்கலம் பொன்னொடு வந்து கறியொடு பெயரும்
arriving with gold and departing with pepper,
drop down on the outward voyage from Nelcynda
the river is full of shoals and the channels are not clear,

english.text: ...the city where the beautiful vessels, the masterpieces of the Yavanas [Ionians/Greeks-Romans], stir white foam on the Culli [Periyar], a river of the Chera, arriving with gold and departing with pepper—when that Muciri, brimming with prosperity, was besieged by the din of war.
english.attribution: Kulke, Hermann & Rothermund, Dietmar, A History of India (Routledge, 2004), as reproduced on Wikipedia (Muziris).

passages.lang_note: Old Tamil is the weakest language in this pipeline. It matched its own probe at cosine 0.368 where Greek, Literary Chinese and Parthian ran 0.61-0.68, and one machine round trip in three came back in the wrong script. Claims resting on this passage are weaker than claims resting on the Greek.

english.text: 55. There is another place at the mouth of this river, the village of Bacare; to which ships drop down on the outward voyage from Nelcynda, and anchor in the roadstead to take on their cargoes; because the river is full of shoals and the channels are not clear. The kings of both these market-towns live in the interior. And as a sign to those approaching these places from the sea there are serpents coming forth to meet you, black in color, but shorter, like snakes in the head, and with blood-red eyes.
english.attribution: Wilfred H. Schoff translation (1912), University of Washington Silk Road Seattle hosted edition.

english.text: §29 Beyond Cana, the land receding greatly, there follows a very deep bay stretching a great way across, which is called Sachalites; and the Frankincense Country, mountainous and forbidding, wrapped in thick clouds and fog, and yielding frankincense from the trees. These incense-bearing trees are not of great height or thickness; they bear the frankincense sticking in drops on the bark, just as the trees among us in Egypt weep their gum. The frankincense is gathered by the King's slaves and those who are sent to this service for punishment. For these places are very unhealthy, and pestilential even to those sailing along the coast, but almost always fatal to those working there, who also perish often from want of food.
english.attribution: Wilfred H. Schoff translation (1912), as adapted/hosted by ToposText.

english.text: In the name of Allah, the Rahman — have mercy upon us, O lord of the heavens; satisfy us by means of your favor; and grant us the essence of it at the end/gift of our days.
english.attribution: Ahmad Al-Jallad, 'A pre-Islamic basmala: reflections on its first epigraphic attestation and its original significance', Jerusalem Studies in Arabic and Islam 52 (2022): 1–28.

english.text: §5 And about eight hundred stadia beyond there is another very deep bay, with a great mound of sand piled up at the right of the entrance; at the bottom of which the opsidian stone is found, and this is the only place where it is produced. These places, from the Calf-Eaters to the other Berber country, are governed by Zoskales, who is miserly in his ways and always striving for more, but otherwise upright, and acquainted with Greek literature.
english.attribution: Wilfred H. Schoff translation (1912), with emendations from Lionel Casson's 1989 Princeton edition, hosted by ToposText.

english.text: §4 Below Ptolemais of the Hunts, at a distance of about three thousand stadia, there is Adulis, a port established by law, lying at the inner end of a bay that runs in toward the south. Before the harbor lies the so-called Mountain Island, about two hundred stadia sea-ward from the very head of the bay, with the shores of the mainland close to it on both sides. Ships bound for this port now anchor here because of attacks from the land. They used formerly to anchor at the very head of the bay, by an island called Diodorus, close to the shore, which could be reached on foot from the land; by which means the barbarous natives attacked the island. Opposite Mountain Island, on the mainland twenty stadia from shore, lies Adulis, a fair-sized village, from which there is a three-days' journey to Coloe, an inland town and the first market for ivory. From that place to the city of the people called Auxumites there is a five days' journey more; to that place all the ivory is brought from the country beyond the Nile through the district called Cyeneum, and thence to Adulis. Practically the whole number of elephants and rhinoceros that are killed live in the places inland, although at rare intervals they are hunted on the seacoast even near Adulis. Before the harbor of that market-town, out at sea on the right hand, there lie a great many little sandy islands called Alalaei, yielding tortoise-shell, which is brought to market there by the Fish-Eaters.
english.attribution: Wilfred H. Schoff translation (1912), with emendations from Lionel Casson's 1989 Princeton edition, hosted by ToposText.
